title: Find a Value of a Mysterious Function Closest to Target
statement:
You are given an integer array `arr` and an integer `target`. For two indices `l` and `r` of `arr` (each from `0` to `arr.length - 1`), the function `func(arr, l, r)` is defined as the bitwise AND `arr[l] & arr[l + 1] & ... & arr[r]` when `l <= r`, and as `-1000000000` when `r < l`.

Over all such pairs `(l, r)`, return the smallest possible value of `|func(arr, l, r) - target|`.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every pair `(l, r)` is O(n²) ANDs, too slow for `10^5` values. (Pairs with `r < l` give `-10^9`, which is never closest because every AND is at least 0 and `target` is at most `10^7`.) The key fact is about bits: extending a subarray can only switch bits off. So among the subarrays that end at one index, the AND values form a chain where each new value drops at least one bit, and since `arr[i] <= 10^6 < 2^20` there are at most about 20 distinct values. Keeping just those distinct values while sweeping right gives every reachable AND.

## Approach

1. `ands` holds the distinct AND values of the subarrays ending at the previous index, from shortest to longest (largest to smallest).
2. For the next `value`, the subarray of length one gives `value` itself; each older result `prev` extends to `prev & value`. Because the list stays ordered, a repeat can only equal the last entry of `next`, so it is skipped.
3. Compare every entry of `next` with `target` and keep the smallest distance in `best`.
4. Replace `ands` with `next` and continue; return `best` at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [9, 12, 3, 7, 15]`, `target = 5`.

- `9`: `next = [9]`, `best = 4`.
- `12`: `next = [12, 9 & 12 = 8]`, distances 7 and 3, `best = 3`.
- `3`: `next = [3, 12 & 3 = 0]` (`8 & 3 = 0` is a repeat), distance 2, `best = 2`.
- `7`: `next = [7, 3, 0]`; `15`: `next = [15, 7, 3, 0]`. Nothing gets closer than 2, so the answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log M), where M is the largest value: each index handles at most about 20 distinct ANDs.
- Space: O(log M) for the two short lists.

## Pitfalls

- Keeping every AND (not just distinct ones) brings back O(n²) work, for example when all values are equal.
- Skipping repeats by looking only at the last entry of `next` is safe because the list stays ordered from largest to smallest; in an unordered list it would miss repeats.
- The closest AND may lie above `target` or below it, so compare every value in `next`, not just the first one that drops below `target`.
- `best` must start larger than any possible distance (up to `10^7`).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `best` | smallest distance to `target` found so far |
| `ands` | distinct AND values of subarrays ending at the previous index |
| `value` | the current element `arr[i]` |
| `next` | distinct AND values of subarrays ending at the current index |
| `prev`, `merged` | an older AND value and that value extended by `value` |
| `result` | one candidate AND value compared with `target` |

narration.2: No distance found yet, so start above every possible one.
narration.3: No subarray ends before the first element, so the list of ANDs starts empty.
narration.4: Sweep the array; value becomes the right end of the subarrays.
narration.5: The subarray holding only value has AND equal to value.
narration.6: Every subarray ending one step earlier can be extended by value.
narration.7: Extending can only switch bits off.
narration.8: The list is ordered, so a repeated AND can only equal the last one kept.
narration.9: Keep only new values: there are at most about 20 per index.
narration.12: Check every AND that ends at this index.
narration.13: Keep the smallest distance to target.
narration.15: These ANDs become the starting point for the next index.
